correctness.rationale: Affine normalization reduces the local Fourier transform to \(P(X,Y)=a+bX+cY+dXY\) on \(\mu_5^2\). If \(ad=bc\), factorization gives exactly 0, 5, or 9 zeros. If \(ad\ne bc\), each row has at most one zero and the zero set is the graph of a Möbius map. Five zeros would make that Möbius map permute the five vertices of the regular pentagon. Since a Möbius map carrying three points of the unit circle to the unit circle carries the whole circle to itself, its induced permutation of the five cyclically ordered vertices preserves or reverses cyclic order and is therefore dihedral. Agreement at three points then forces the map to be \(X\mapsto\eta X\) or \(X\mapsto\eta/X\), whose coefficient identities force two of \(a,b,c,d\) to vanish, a contradiction. Hence the nonfactorable case has at most four zeros. The seven supplied exact cyclotomic witnesses attain zero counts \(0,1,2,3,4,5,9\); the actual verifier checks these in \(\mathbb Q(\zeta_5)\) and exhausts all 120 pentagon permutations by exact cross ratios. Each local frequency has \(5^{d-2}\) ambient fibers, proving the all-dimensional spectrum.

value.rationale: A fixed-support Fourier spectrum is a natural refinement of the finite uncertainty problem: it measures how support geometry changes rank deficiency beyond global cardinality bounds. The theorem completely resolves the smallest nontrivial two-dimensional four-point parallelogram case over \(\mathbb F_5\), including a genuine forbidden band and exact witnesses.
residual_risks: The result is specific to one prime and one four-point geometry.

final_claim: For every \(d\ge2\), a complex-valued function on \(\mathbb F_5^d\) supported exactly on an affine parallelogram \(x+\{0,u,v,u+v\}\), with \(u,v\) independent and all four support values nonzero, has Fourier-support size exactly one of \(\{16,20,21,22,23,24,25\}5^{d-2}\), and every listed value occurs.
limitations: Only exact four-point affine-parallelogram supports over \(\mathbb F_5\) are classified.
The theorem does not classify arbitrary four-point geometries or other primes.
